newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Triple murderer faces deportation to Britain.
newsitem.headline: Triple murderer faces deportation to Britain.

text.p: Convicted triple murderer Archie "Mad Dog" McCafferty is likely to be deported from Australia to Britain within weeks after he was granted parole on Friday following 23 years in jail.
Australian Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock said a deportation order had already been signed, while British Consul-General Philip Morrice said outside the court that Britain accepted the decision.

Glasgow-born McCafferty, 49, was given three life sentences in 1974 as the leader of a gang which killed three men over five days in Australia in 1973. While in jail McCafferty was also convicted of manslaughter over the death of another prisoner.
Local media nicknamed him "Mad Dog" because of his killings.
The New South Wales Parole Board on Friday granted McCafferty parole, after four earlier parole bids had been rejected, and ordered him released by May 3.
"We would expect at the point in time when he is released from detention that the (deportation) order should be carried out," Ruddock told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio.
McCafferty came to Australia as a 10-year-old with his family but never became an Australian citizen.
He has lodged an appeal with Australia's Administrative Appeals Tribunal in an effort to halt his deportation, while his likely return has sparked opposition in Britain.
Glasgow MP Michael Martin has appealed to Australia not to "use the United Kingdom as a dumping ground".

The random murders which led to McCafferty's life sentence began after he said he suffered a delusion while visiting the grave of his baby son -- who suffocated while breastfeeding -- telling him to kill seven people.

He remained obsessed with the number seven in prison, writing an autobiography entitled "Seven Shall Die" and was initially considered an aggressive and extemely dangerous prisoner, parole board judge Des Ward said on Friday.
However, Ward said by 1988 McCafferty was seen as a model prisoner and numerous assessments had described him as quiet and co-operative, and as able to relate to people normally.
He had shown no evidence of pyschiatric disorder and had successfully spent four months on work release since late 1996.
McCafferty, dressed in jeans and a blue prison shirt and tie, apologised to relatives of his victims in court, saying he was "out of touch with reality" at the time of the killings.

"All I can do is offer you my sincere apologies," he said. "If I could give my life to bring your fathers back I would do that gladly." McCafferty said he was a changed man and deserved a second chance at life.
